novel_idea.topic_thesis: Agent permissions should expire when the doctrine supporting them exceeds its half-life, because stale doctrine turns faithful execution into confident error.
novel_idea.angle: Treat autonomous authority as conditional on doctrine freshness, not as a permanent reward for passing capability evaluations. Bind permissions to a doctrine version and reduce them when that doctrine is no longer current.
novel_idea.hook: Your AI agent’s permission should expire before its doctrine becomes history.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Autonomous agents act from organizational doctrine, but doctrine ages as markets, obligations, and operating reality change. An agent can continue passing task-level evaluations while executing premises that are no longer valid. Because agents apply those premises quickly and consistently, stale doctrine can produce coherent wrongness at scale. The operator decision is to make permissions version-bound and time-limited: when the supporting doctrine reaches the end of its declared half-life, authority falls to a lower permission level until an owner revalidates the doctrine against current reality feedback and evaluations.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest prior post argues that reality feedback must be able to revise false doctrine before AI scales coherent wrongness. This argument adds a different control mechanism and operator decision: autonomous permission should decay automatically with doctrine age, even before a visible failure arrives. It treats doctrine freshness as a continuing condition of authority rather than relying only on downstream contradiction to trigger correction.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines doctrine half-life as how long doctrine remains valid, current, and understood before drift or world change makes it stale. It requires current, versioned, owned doctrine; risk-proportional permissions; update cadence; and accountability when doctrine ages but an agent keeps acting. It also states that stale doctrine can be worse than no doctrine because a false model regulates confidently, and that permissions should rise only as doctrine, evaluations, and reality feedback mature.

payload.body_text:
An agent can pass every evaluation and still become unsafe without changing at all.

Doctrine has a half-life: the period it remains valid, current, and understood before reality or organizational drift makes it stale.

That matters because stale doctrine can be worse than none. A false model regulates confidently. The agent follows instructions faithfully while customers, constraints, or strategy have already moved.

Permissions should therefore attach to a doctrine version, not permanently to the agent. When that version exceeds its half-life, authority should step down automatically—from acting to drafting, or from drafting to suggesting—until the doctrine is reconstituted and tested.

If doctrine expires but authority does not, you have automated yesterday’s judgment.
